summary: The risen Jesus appears to James, His brother, who had not believed in Him during His ministry. Paul records the meeting in a single line.
key_insight: James grew up in the same home as Jesus and did not believe in Him (John 7:5). Later he led the church in Jerusalem. The only thing Scripture records to explain the change is one line from Paul: “He was seen by James.”
story: James was the first named of Jesus’ brothers, raised in the same household in Nazareth. During Jesus’ ministry His brothers did not believe in Him. Once His own people went out to take hold of Him, saying that He was out of His mind.

After the resurrection, Jesus appeared to James. Paul records it in his list of witnesses: “After that He was seen by James, then by all the apostles.” No Gospel describes the meeting, and Paul does not say where or when it happened.

Within weeks, Jesus’ brothers were among the believers praying in Jerusalem with Mary and the apostles. James became a leader of the church there, and he is generally understood to be the James who wrote the letter that bears his name, calling himself a bondservant of the Lord Jesus Christ.

scene.label: Which James?
scene.text: Several men in the New Testament were named James. James the son of Zebedee was one of the Twelve, already covered in Paul’s list. This James is almost certainly the brother of Jesus, whom Paul met in Jerusalem and called “James, the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19).

scene.label: Brothers who doubted
scene.text: John says plainly, “even His brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5). They urged Jesus to go to Judea and show Himself to the world, words that sound more like a challenge than faith.

scene.label: A pillar in Jerusalem
scene.text: James spoke decisively at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21), and Paul names him first of the three “pillars” of the church, ahead of Cephas and John (Galatians 2:9). When Peter escaped from prison, he said, “Go, tell these things to James” (Acts 12:17).

scene.label: His death
scene.text: The Jewish historian Josephus records that James was stoned in Jerusalem about AD 62, on the orders of the high priest Ananus. Early Christian writers remembered him as a man of prayer who died faithful to Christ.

seeing.reveals: Jesus did not leave His unbelieving brother to be argued into faith by others; He showed Himself to James. The grace of the risen Lord reached into His own family and turned a skeptic into a servant.
seeing.living: James knew Jesus longer than any disciple did and apparently did not believe until he met Him risen. Being close to the things of Jesus is not the same as trusting Him. Those who grew up around the faith, and those praying for relatives who have not believed, can take heart: the risen Lord sought out the doubter in His own household.
seeing.ponder: Have you lived so close to the things of Jesus that you have never truly met Him yourself? Or whom in your family are you praying He will meet?

preaching.big_idea: The risen Jesus made His doubting brother a servant, and His grace still reaches skeptics close to home.
outline: A brother who once did not believe (7)
A persecutor called last of all (8–9)
Grace that makes us what we are (10–11)
preaching.watch_for: Paul’s list closes with two men who had once stood outside: James, who did not believe in his brother (John 7:5), and Paul, who “persecuted the church of God” (15:9). Paul explains his own change in words that fit James as well: “by the grace of God I am what I am” (15:10).
